title: Text and Domain-Specific Features
learning_outcomes: Explain text and domain-specific features and accurately refer to at least two syllabus subtopics.
Apply the main idea of text and domain-specific features to a small example, trace, calculation, or scenario.
Identify one important assumption or failure mode and describe how to check it.

content.intro: In this lesson, you will study text and domain-specific features in the context of feature engineering and feature selection. You will connect the PDF subtopics to a small example and practice describing what the evidence does—and does not—support.
content.why_it_matters: Text and Domain-Specific Features matters because it affects how data is collected, represented, analyzed, interpreted, or used in a decision. Check the task and assumptions before choosing a method.

content_blocks.title: The central idea
content_blocks.text: Features encode information a model can use at prediction time. Every derived field needs consistent production logic and a check against target leakage.

items.title: Text length and token counts
items.text: Define text length and token counts in relation to text and domain-specific features; identify the input, output, assumptions, and who uses the result.

items.title: Keyword indicators
items.text: Work through keyword indicators using a small, synthetic example before scaling up. State what the calculation or method returns and why that result is useful.

items.title: Domain knowledge
items.text: Check the edge cases for domain knowledge: missing values, unusual ranges, different groups, time boundaries, or a changed input can affect the conclusion.

items.title: Feature crosses
items.text: Document the rule or choice for feature crosses so another learner can reproduce the analysis and understand its limitations.

content_blocks.title: Guided walkthrough
content_blocks.text: 1. Restate the question addressed by text and domain-specific features. 2. Identify the input data, intended output, and assumptions. 3. Predict what the small example should show before reading its output. 4. Change one input or assumption, compare the result, and document what remains uncertain.

content_blocks.reset_steps: Restore the provided synthetic input, rerun or retrace the example, and change one value at a time. Do not use personal records, credentials, or data you are not authorized to access.

content_blocks.title: Common mistakes and fixes
content_blocks.text: Keep the question, data grain, units, and assumptions explicit. If a result differs, inspect the input and steps in order. Avoid turning an observed association into a causal claim, treating a sample as the population, or assuming a small demonstration guarantees production behavior. Scaling may matter for distance-based methods; fit preprocessing using training data only.

content_blocks.title: Responsible interpretation
content_blocks.text: This example is a teaching aid. It is static in the CodeLeaf lesson and is not executed in the browser. It uses small synthetic values; validate any real workflow in a separate, appropriate local environment and protect sensitive data.

task_acceptance_criteria: Refer accurately to the topic and its syllabus subtopics.

Document at least one assumption, limitation, data-quality issue, or evaluation check.
hints: Write down the input, expected result, units, and assumptions first.
Change only one condition when testing a revised example.
Ask whether the data and method represent the real decision; do not infer causality or production readiness from a toy example.
troubleshooting: Check input values, path assumptions, package versions, indentation, and units.
